title: Geography of Global Conflict

jokes.text: Annie answers the teacher's question perfectly, only to be immediately interrupted and corrected — the teacher was calling on 'Annie Kim,' not Annie Edison
jokes.setup: Professor calls on 'Annie' and Annie Edison immediately launches into a confident, complete, correct answer about the Yalta Conference
jokes.punchline: Professor interrupts mid-answer: 'I'm sorry. Annie Kim.' — the identical name creates an identity-swap humiliation for Annie Edison
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly economical cold open joke. The setup is entirely silent — we don't know there's another Annie. The punchline lands with almost surgical precision mid-sentence, maximizing the humiliation. It also immediately plants the rivalry premise. The character integration is high: this only works because Annie Edison is the type-A overachiever who would launch into a full answer the instant her name is called. Strong structural craft.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Wow. Okay, I'm going to have to break your legs and put you in a wheelchair just to make you cool.

jokes.text: Annie Kim continues with the same answer Annie Edison was giving, word-for-word correctly, including the 'spoiler alert' side note
jokes.setup: Annie Edison was cut off mid-answer; Annie Kim picks up seamlessly
jokes.punchline: Annie Kim adds a smug 'Side note' that shows she had even more prepared — she out-Annies Annie
jokes.explanation: The doubling-down escalation is well-earned. Annie Kim doesn't just answer — she answers better, with a 'side note' that Annie didn't have. This efficiently establishes the nemesis dynamic in seconds. The joke is structural: same content, different speaker, plus bonus insight = comedic domination.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I got this see-through yellow pen so I can color in the words.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You mean highlight?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What? No, highlight is my favorite thing.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Oh, boy, spoiler alert. Somebody just won a ride in the wheelchair.'
jokes.setup: Annie Kim's academic performance just crushed Annie Edison in front of the class; tension is building
jokes.punchline: Pierce's non-sequitur threat to give someone a 'ride in the wheelchair' — implying violence — as a reaction to academic competition
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce: disproportionate threat delivered with absurd specificity. The wheelchair detail elevates it from a generic threat to something distinctly Pierce-flavored — dark, oblivious to social norms, and vaguely menacing. Good economy; works as a punctuation beat on the cold open rivalry setup.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Finally, some real equipment! A badge, a baton, a radio... Oh man, I've been waiting for this moment my whole life.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know what this means? I can finally use force. Legally. On people. Beautiful.

jokes.text: Pierce to Britta: 'I'm proud of you for deciding on a major, Britta. I'd like to thank the lord in my prayers about you, but you're still dressing like a streetwalker.'
jokes.setup: Pierce opens with what sounds like a genuine compliment about Britta's maturity
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts it with a gratuitous insult about her clothing — classic Pierce unable to give an unqualified compliment
jokes.explanation: The structure is reliable Pierce: genuine attempt at warmth sabotaged by an outdated insult. The 'I'd like to thank the lord in my prayers about you' is an unusually specific and funny construction before the pivot. Character integration is high — this joke only works in Pierce's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You see this badge? It says 'Have a nice day.' I'm not a real cop.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We know, Chang.

jokes.text: Britta: 'I got one of those see-through yellow pens so I can do that thing where you color in the words.' Jeff: 'Highlight?' Britta: 'Probably the backpack.'
jokes.setup: Britta is excitedly listing her new school supplies as proof of her academic commitment; Jeff corrects her not knowing the word 'highlight'
jokes.punchline: When Jeff says 'Highlight?' Britta ignores the correction and pivots to 'Probably the backpack' — refusing to acknowledge she didn't know the word, redirecting to what she's most proud of
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a quintessential Community construction. Britta not knowing the word 'highlight' is funny on its own, but the genius is her response to being corrected: she doesn't acknowledge Jeff's correction at all, just pivots to 'Probably the backpack' — a non-answer that reveals she heard him, didn't process it, and moved on. This is deeply character-specific: Britta's particular brand of enthusiastic incompetence. The economy is exceptional — four words create a complete comedic portrait. Highly quotable, rewatch bonus because you catch more layers.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Please, I need this equipment. I use it for... educational purposes. And recreational purposes. And... intimate purposes.

jokes.text: Britta sees a 'Free the Damascus Three' flier, recognizes a friend imprisoned in Syria, and immediately pivots to existential guilt: 'She's imprisoned by an oppressive regime halfway around the world and I'm, what? In college?'
jokes.setup: Britta has just been proudly showing off her new school supplies as signs of maturity
jokes.punchline: She immediately collapses into performative guilt about her comfortable college life vs. her imprisoned activist friend
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta self-flagellation. The juxtaposition of her pride in a backpack vs. her friend's imprisonment is funny, but the joke is somewhat expected given Britta's established character. It sets up the episode's B-plot well but isn't particularly surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, this is great. We're really making progress on diversity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We have two Annies now. Annie and... evil Annie.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Man, she's got a Facebook group?' — reacting to her imprisoned friend's online presence while seemingly forgetting the gravity of the imprisonment
jokes.setup: Britta has just been agonizing about her friend's imprisonment by an oppressive regime
jokes.punchline: She immediately deflates the moment by being impressed/distracted that her imprisoned friend has a Facebook group
jokes.explanation: Sharp little undercut. The bathos of going from imprisoned-by-regime to impressed-by-Facebook is well-timed and character-specific. The joke captures the millennial activist's contradiction: deeply moved by injustice, immediately mediated by social media. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Annie, you're going to face some serious competition out there. I'm not going to lie to you.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: From who?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: From women.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's... that's sexist, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm not sexist. I'm not saying women are worse than men. I'm just saying they're different. And that difference is that they're women.

jokes.text: Chang, holding a police flashlight: 'My first cop flashlight. Can't wait to get some brains on this bad boy.'
jokes.setup: Chang has apparently just been hired as campus security and is inspecting his equipment
jokes.punchline: He enthusiastically anticipates using the flashlight to bash heads — revealing his power-mad nature immediately
jokes.explanation: Chang's deranged enthusiasm for violence is immediately established. 'Get some brains on this bad boy' is a funny specific — not 'use it' but specifically wanting blood/brains on it. Character integration is strong; this is entirely Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, I remember freshman year Annie. She was like you, but angrier, and on several medications.

jokes.text: Chang reads his security badge: 'The badge says to serve and protect!' [pause] 'No, it doesn't.' 'How's my smile?' Oh, man.
jokes.setup: Chang is excited about his new security guard role and invokes the classic police motto
jokes.punchline: His superior flatly corrects him — the badge actually says 'How's my smile?' — revealing the comedic indignity of the campus security position
jokes.explanation: Excellent deflation joke. The setup is Chang's delusion of grandeur (invoking cop mythology), the punchline is the deeply mundane reality of Greendale's customer-service-focused security operation. 'How's my smile?' is a perfect specific — it's the kind of badge a Denny's manager would have, not a cop. The 'Oh, man' reaction from Chang lands the final beat. High economy, strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The rainforests are disappearing because of corporate greed and government corruption. They're cutting down trees to make room for cattle ranches owned by people who don't even care about the environment. It's all connected to pharmaceutical companies who want to suppress natural remedies because they can't patent trees. Wake up, sheeple! Look it up.

jokes.text: Security Chief tells Chang his job is to guard a garbage can that students bump into coming out of the library: 'You can serve and protect them from a nasty boo-boo.'
jokes.setup: Chang asks 'What the hell am I in charge of?' expecting some real authority
jokes.punchline: His entire jurisdiction is a single trash can near the library exit, described with mock-heroic language ('serve and protect them from a nasty boo-boo')
jokes.explanation: Good institutional comedy — Greendale's pathetic infrastructure reduces Chang's power fantasy to babysitting a trash can. The 'nasty boo-boo' language is a funny tonal choice, treating a trivial thing with bureaucratic gravity.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Britta, did you wake up on the wrong side of the bed?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: There is no wrong side of the bed, Troy. That's just a saying designed to make people feel bad about their natural sleep patterns.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So you woke up on the regular side?

jokes.text: Chang asks 'What do I do if I see a crime?' Chief: 'What a security guard does — Call a cop.'
jokes.setup: Chang is being briefed on his security duties, implying he has actual law enforcement power
jokes.punchline: The punchline undercuts any authority: his entire job in an emergency is to call someone else
jokes.explanation: Functional deflation joke about the impotence of campus security. Less inventive than the badge joke that precedes it, but it completes the picture effectively. The rhythm of the exchange is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I've spent my whole life trying to find my purpose, you know? I've been a cop, a psychologist, a therapist... and every time I think I'm on the right path, something goes wrong. But that's not going to stop me anymore. I'm taking control of my destiny, and anyone who stands in my way can just... can just go f— uh... frick themselves.

jokes.text: Chang, begging to keep the handcuffs: 'Please? I swear they're just for sex!'
jokes.setup: Chang's superior takes away his handcuffs as part of the depowering process
jokes.punchline: Chang's defense — that they're only for personal sexual use — is meant to be reassuring but is actually more alarming and reveals TMI about Chang
jokes.explanation: Very sharp. The logic is impeccable from Chang's perspective — he's trying to be reassuring — but the reassurance makes everything worse. The economy is near-perfect: six words that tell you everything about Chang's psychology. High quotability because the line is self-contained and surprising. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta's going to get herself killed doing whatever dangerous activist thing she's doing now. She'll probably mess it up though. Britta fails at everything she tries to do that's remotely rebellious or important.

jokes.text: Jeff's talking head introduction: 'And this ragtag group of cut-ups is my study group.' — delivered over what is presumably the group being chaotic or mundane
jokes.setup: Standard sitcom 'meet the gang' beat
jokes.punchline: Jeff's weary, slightly contemptuous framing of his own friends as 'cut-ups' — the word choice is both affectionate and dismissive
jokes.explanation: Mild joke — Jeff's sardonic framing of the group is consistent with his character but not particularly inventive. Functions as scene-setting with mild comedic flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: His entire job is just warning people about a garbage can

jokes.text: Annie Kim and Annie Edison's GPA battle: 'Well, mine was higher if you consider my school's ranking.' / 'Well, it sounds like you had a lighter course load.' / 'Well, I was in a lot of clubs. I founded 17 of them.'
jokes.setup: Two overachievers who share a name try to establish academic dominance through increasingly petty metrics
jokes.punchline: The escalation from GPA to school ranking to course load to 'I founded 17 clubs' — each one-upping more desperately
jokes.explanation: The 'founded 17 clubs' is the standout specific here — it's funny because it's so precise and yet so transparently a brag about resume-padding. The whole exchange is a sharp observation about the kind of academic competition that happens between high achievers. Strong character integration: only two Annies could have this fight.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You better watch yourself, Perry. These streets are dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well maybe I like danger. Maybe I'm into it. Maybe I'm a rebel who does... rebel things... dangerously.

jokes.text: Annie suggests founding a model U.N. then immediately dismisses Annie Kim: 'I'll probably be busy, and you probably need to study, so see you in class. Okay, goodbye.'
jokes.setup: Annie presents the model U.N. idea as a friendly, open invitation
jokes.punchline: She immediately shuts down Annie Kim's interest with passive-aggressive dismissals before she can even respond, then exits preemptively
jokes.explanation: Annie's oblivious competitiveness is well-captured here. She invites Annie Kim and in the same breath tries to preemptively exclude her. The 'Okay, goodbye' self-dismissal is a funny kicker — she ends the conversation for both of them without being asked.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I could meet Ban Ki-moon, or Kofi Annan, or Will.I.Am.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Will.I.Am is not a UN diplomat.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, not with that attitude.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Wow, Annie. How progressive of you to have a multicultural evil twin.' / Troy: 'An Asian Annie.' / Pierce: 'Obama's America.'
jokes.setup: The group has just watched Annie's tense interaction with Annie Kim
jokes.punchline: Three different comic registers: Jeff's mock-progressive framing, Troy's reductive observation, Pierce's dated political non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Three-part joke structure that uses character voices efficiently. Jeff's 'multicultural evil twin' is the wittiest; Troy's 'An Asian Annie' is a perfect straight-man reduplication; Pierce's 'Obama's America' is the capper — a catch-all reaction for anything he doesn't understand. Each character's voice is distinct. 'Obama's America' is quotable as a standalone Pierce-ism.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: I have extensive experience with Model U.N. In fact, they used to call me 'The Diplomat.'

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: Though, to be fair, that was mostly because I kept accidentally sitting on the chairs.

jokes.text: Pierce warns Annie about Annie Kim: 'You be careful, Annie. They are ruthless.' / Annie: 'What?' / Pierce: 'What? Not Asians. Women.'
jokes.setup: Pierce issues a vague warning that sounds like it's going to be a racist generalization
jokes.punchline: He corrects himself — 'Not Asians. Women.' — which is both a subversion and arguably equally problematic, capturing Pierce's particular brand of oblivious sexism
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's craftiest jokes. The structure is a fake-out: Pierce sounds like he's about to say something racist, the correction ('Not Asians') seems like a redemption, but 'Women' reveals he's replaced one prejudice with another — and is completely blind to this. The economy is exceptional: five words execute a full Pierce character study. The beat relies on the audience anticipating the racist punchline and being delivered something technically different but structurally equivalent. High quotability, strong rewatch value because it's layered.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what's the professor's name?

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: It's Pubis. Professor Pubis.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Like... pubis?

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: It's pronounced 'PEW-bis,' actually.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Sure, that's definitely going to catch on.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: My family name has been mispronounced for generations, and frankly, I'm tired of the smirking.

jokes.text: Annie insists she finds Annie Kim 'adorable' and 'like a younger me' while having visibly just been hostile to her
jokes.setup: Annie tries to frame her reaction to Annie Kim as benign affection
jokes.punchline: The gap between her claimed attitude ('I find her adorable') and her obvious behavior (passive aggression, dismissal) is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom irony — character's self-perception vs. reality. Well-executed but not exceptionally original. It works because Annie's obliviousness is a consistent character trait.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: I am Clark M. Eichelburger, founder of the United Nations.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: I've dedicated my entire life to studying and honoring his legacy. Every waking moment is consumed by his achievements, his vision, his... his very existence.

jokes.text: Jeff reminds Annie of her Adderall incident: 'You mean the younger you that took so much Adderall she tried to straighten the lines on our high school football field during a game?'
jokes.setup: Annie romanticizes her younger self as the model for Annie Kim
jokes.punchline: Jeff's callback to Annie's Adderall addiction backstory reframes 'younger Annie' as a drug-fueled chaos agent — the specific image of straightening football field lines during a live game is vivid and absurd
jokes.explanation: Strong use of show mythology. The specific image — straightening lines on a football field during a game — is both hilarious and plausible as an Adderall-driven compulsion. It's character-specific, pays off established backstory, and deflates Annie's nostalgia beautifully. Good rewatch bonus for viewers who know the Season 1 context.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: She's such a b— busybody.

jokes.text: Pierce rallies to Annie's defense: 'That little twerp is a can of Annie lite. She couldn't hold a candle to the real thing in any category of anything.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is trying to be supportive of Annie against Annie Kim
jokes.punchline: 'Annie lite' as a brand comparison is an oddly specific and funny way to diminish someone; 'in any category of anything' is a hilariously vague superlative
jokes.explanation: Pierce's brand-comparison insult ('Annie lite') is a funny specific and his follow-up 'in any category of anything' is endearingly inarticulate. The joke works partly because Pierce means it as a compliment while being inadvertently dismissive of Annie Kim.

dialogue.speaker: Annie Kim
dialogue.line: I started Model U.N. at Greendale!

dialogue.speaker: Annie Edison
dialogue.line: No, I did. I've been running it for years.

dialogue.speaker: Annie Kim
dialogue.line: Well, I'm the real Annie Kim, so it's mine.

dialogue.speaker: Annie Edison
dialogue.line: That's not how intellectual property works.

dialogue.speaker: Annie Kim
dialogue.line: I called it first. Finders keepers.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'You know what else was the best? The rainforests. Too bad the fascist oligarchies are raping them to make hamburgers. Look it up.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just finished an earnest compliment to Annie
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to an unrelated, conspiratorial rant about rainforest destruction, delivered with the same earnest authority — 'Look it up' as an ominous instruction
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce non-sequitur. The pivot from complimenting Annie to hamburger-rainforest conspiracy is jarring in a funny way. 'Look it up' as a punctuation mark on the rant is a characteristic Pierce move — he's not explaining further, he's assigning homework. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: So Jeff, Annie... you two aren't... you know?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No! She's like... she's like a daughter to me.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: He's like a father figure.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: That's not better.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Looks like someone woke up on the regular side of the bed.' — responding to Britta's existential crisis about her imprisoned friend
jokes.setup: Britta is spiraling about her activist past vs. her current comfortable college life
jokes.punchline: Shirley's inversion of 'wrong side of the bed' — 'regular side' — implies the problem is Britta's normalcy, not her mood
jokes.explanation: Smart wordplay. 'Regular side of the bed' is a clever inversion that implies Britta's distress comes from being too normal — a precise observation about her character. Economy is high: a single phrase does real comedic and thematic work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're just friends.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Best friends?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Friends who happen to... spend a lot of time together.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Friends with history?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Friends with... complicated history.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: So like, best friends?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why do you keep saying that?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Because you're being weird about it!

jokes.text: Britta: 'I haven't been tear-gassed in so long.' — delivered as wistful nostalgia
jokes.setup: Shirley mentions that Britta's friend was tear-gassed and beaten
jokes.punchline: Britta responds with wistful, almost nostalgic regret about not having been tear-gassed recently — treating a traumatic experience as a lifestyle marker she misses
jokes.explanation: Exceptional single-line joke. The delivery implied by the script is wistful nostalgia — she misses being tear-gassed the way someone might miss their college band or an ex. This is deeply character-specific Britta: her activist credentials are a point of pride and longing. The economy is perfect — the whole joke is seven words. Highly quotable, strong character integration. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Did you know Somalia has no central government? It's a failed state! And the piracy! The piracy is incredible!

jokes.text: Shirley's new-path speech: 'Oh, goody, a new path. Is it lined with credit cards and flat screen TVs? Does it go by an Ikea?'
jokes.setup: Shirley tries to steer Britta toward her 'new path' of responsible adulthood
jokes.punchline: Britta sarcastically lists the consumerist symbols of bourgeois adulthood — credit cards, flat-screen TVs, Ikea — as the destination of the 'new path'
jokes.explanation: Good Britta voice. The escalation from credit cards to flat-screen TVs to Ikea (a step down in terms of prestige, which makes it funnier) works as a portrait of Britta's contempt for consumerism. The specificity of 'Does it go by an Ikea?' is the best element.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Somalia is a paradise.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Maybe my path is a war path that leads to the terrordome, n-words!'
jokes.setup: Britta is escalating her protest rhetoric in front of her study group
jokes.punchline: She invokes Public Enemy's 'Fight the Power' / 'Welcome to the Terrordome' but self-censors the N-word, rendering her edgy rallying cry immediately awkward and deflated
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Britta's 'terrordome, n-words' is a perfect encapsulation of her character: she wants to be radical and street-credible but can't commit to the actual language, so she says 'n-words' — which is both more offensive in its awkwardness and more revealing of her privilege. The self-correction in the next line ('Okay, maybe I went too far') deepens the joke. High originality, strong structure, deeply character-specific. The escalation from 'war path' to 'terrordome' to 'n-words' follows perfect comedic logic.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, Georgia? I thought we were talking about the country!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Well bless your heart, y'all. Georgia is a fine state with pecan pie and sweet tea.

jokes.text: Britta's immediate follow-up talking head: 'Okay, maybe I went too far. Maybe I don't want to offend my African-American friends, but the larger point is, maybe I'm not done raging against the machine.'
jokes.setup: Britta just yelled 'terrordome, n-words' at her friends
jokes.punchline: In her confessional, she partially walks it back but reasserts her activist bona fides — the self-awareness is selective and reveals the core delusion
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke. The confessional format lets Britta explain herself in a way that makes things worse. Her concern is specifically about offending 'my African-American friends' (not about the broader use) and her reassertion that she's 'raging against the machine' shows the narcissistic core of her activism.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This Model U.N. scenario has a logical inconsistency. The resolution references Article 51 of the UN Charter, but the fictional country we're representing didn't exist until 1993, making the reference anachronistic.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: Yes, well... good catch, I suppose.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Raging against the what? That sounds dangerous.' Shirley: 'Don't worry. She'll be bad at it.'
jokes.setup: Britta has declared she's going to 'rage against the machine'
jokes.punchline: Pierce's literal misunderstanding ('raging against the what?') followed by Shirley's devastating prediction ('She'll be bad at it') — the latter being a perfect Shirley line
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke with distinct character voices. Pierce's literalism is a standard Pierce move; Shirley's 'She'll be bad at it' is the stronger punchline — it's simultaneously an insult and an observation, delivered with Shirley's characteristic gentle certainty. The prediction also sets up the B-plot payoff. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You can't cage freedom! I'm like a... a bald eagle wrapped in the American flag, but the flag is also a cage, and the cage is the American flag, and I'm the freedom that's being caged by the very symbol of freedom!

jokes.text: Chang's visual running gag begins: 'Keep clear of the can. Sir, step around the can.' — Chang solemnly guarding the garbage can
jokes.setup: Chang was assigned to guard a garbage can outside the library
jokes.punchline: He is actually doing it, with full authoritative seriousness
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the trash can setup is satisfying. Chang's complete earnestness about an absurd task is funny. This is the first beat in what becomes a visual running gag through the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, wait! Is anyone live-tweeting this? Someone Snapchat it! Post it on Instagram!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is oppression! People need to see this! Hashtag free Britta!

jokes.text: Britta singing Lionel Richie's 'Hello' loudly in the hallway as a protest; Chang gives her a warning
jokes.setup: Britta has decided to 'rage against the machine' via campus protest; Chang is guarding his can
jokes.punchline: Her chosen form of protest is singing Lionel Richie — deeply uncool, unheroic, and bewildering as an act of rebellion; Chang's stern 'You just got yourself a warning' treats it as a serious security threat
jokes.explanation: Absurdist comedy with strong character logic. Britta's protest is Lionel Richie — it's the most un-threatening, unhip form of rebellion possible, which is exactly right for who Britta is. Chang's 'You just got yourself a warning' plays it completely straight, which amplifies the absurdity. Good rewatch value because the Lionel Richie motif pays off repeatedly.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Uruguay's delegate is recognized.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: The delegation from [homophobic slur that sounds like Uruguay] moves to—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's Uruguay, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's what I said, [repeats slur].

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, you're saying it wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: [Says slur again], right?

jokes.text: Britta: 'I piss warnings, pig.' — responding to Chang's security warning while continuing to sing
jokes.setup: Chang has warned Britta about her singing protest
jokes.punchline: Britta's response attempts edgy confrontational protest language but is undermined by the context (singing Lionel Richie to a mall-cop equivalent)
jokes.explanation: Good Britta line — the aggression of 'I piss warnings, pig' vs. the absurdity of the situation (Lionel Richie protest vs. Chang) creates effective comic dissonance. 'I piss warnings' is a funny construction, trying too hard to be hard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Did you just...?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No. No way.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That happened.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Lord have mercy!

jokes.text: Chang's 'I got my eye on you, missy' — final beat of the Britta/Chang confrontation
jokes.setup: Chang and Britta have had a tense standoff over her Lionel Richie protest
jokes.punchline: 'Missy' as Chang's attempt at threatening law-enforcement authority — it's the least intimidating possible word choice
jokes.explanation: Light button joke on the Chang/Britta scene. 'Missy' deflates whatever tension the standoff built. Functional but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Dean, I'm bringing Britta in for making a mess.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Chang, I don't have time for this. Britta, you're free to go.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: But Dean, I'm the security guard. I have authority here.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: No, you don't.

jokes.text: Pierce's 'Sneak attack. That's just like— Not women, Asians.' reaction to Annie Kim stealing the model U.N. idea
jokes.setup: The group learns Annie Kim stole the model U.N. idea; Pierce starts to issue a generalization
jokes.punchline: He self-corrects from 'women' to 'Asians' — reversing his earlier correction (joke 17) and completing the callback
jokes.explanation: Brilliant callback structure. In joke 17, Pierce corrected himself from an implied racist generalization to a sexist one. Here, the reverse happens — he starts with sexism and corrects to racism. The flip is structurally elegant and shows the writers thinking architecturally about the episode. It also works as a standalone because it establishes Pierce as an equal-opportunity bigot who can't settle on which group to blame. High marks across all craft dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Dean, Dean! We need to talk about the parking lot. There's this... this metal thing that goes up and down, you know? It's red and white striped, and it blocks cars from going through, and when you push a button or something it just... rises up into the air like it's surrendering.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Chang, that's a parking arm.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I know what it is, I'm just describing it to you!

jokes.text: Jeff: 'And meet Kofi Annan, Boutros Boutros Ghali, and Will.I.Am.' — listing the prizes of winning the model U.N.
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why winning the model U.N. matters — the networking opportunities with UN luminaries
jokes.punchline: Will.I.Am appears as a UN luminary alongside actual former UN Secretaries-General — a category error that reveals the absurdity of Greendale's aspirations
jokes.explanation: Good list joke with a classic misdirection structure: two legitimate UN luminaries, then Will.I.Am. The specificity of 'Boutros Boutros Ghali' (which even gets its own beat) is funny, and Will.I.Am as the third represents the hilarious gap between prestige aspiration and Greendale reality.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, I have a theory. What if one of us is actually dead and we just don't know it yet? Like, what if the smell is just... us decomposing?

jokes.text: Pierce reacts to 'Boutros Boutros Ghali': his confusion at the double-first-name
jokes.setup: Jeff lists 'Boutros Boutros Ghali' as a potential contact
jokes.punchline: Pierce's visibly confused reaction beat to the repeated name — the audience sees his confusion even before Jeff says 'I'm gonna find this little brat's off-switch'
jokes.explanation: Light reaction beat. Pierce's confusion at the repeated-name is a quick visual/reaction joke that works in the rhythm of the scene. Not exceptional but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to be the bigger person here. I'm mature enough to rise above this petty bickering.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're a big stupid head with a stupid face and stupid hair!

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I'm gonna find this little brat's off-switch.' Jeff: 'Jeff!' Pierce: 'He's just being protective. I'll stop him.'
jokes.setup: The group is debating how to respond to Annie Kim's model U.N. coup
jokes.punchline: Jeff claims Pierce is 'just being protective' and that he'll 'stop him' — but Jeff immediately goes to find Annie Kim himself, suggesting he's equally invested
jokes.explanation: Light joke on Jeff's self-awareness vs. his actual behavior. The 'He's just being protective. I'll stop him.' followed by Jeff presumably marching off to do the same thing is a good ironic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, Annie, calm down. You're being a little too... intense.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Too intense? Jeff, you literally told me I needed to be more assertive!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I said assertive, not... hot.

jokes.text: Professor Cligoris's name — and the Professor's immediate acknowledgment: 'Either pronunciation is fine?'
jokes.setup: Jeff addresses the professor by name
jokes.punchline: The name sounds like 'clitoris'; the professor preemptively addresses the pronunciation issue with practiced weariness ('Either pronunciation is fine?')
jokes.explanation: The joke's strength is not the name itself (which is a cheap pun) but the professor's response — 'Either pronunciation is fine?' shows this is a man who has lived with this name his whole life and developed a weary, accommodating response to it. That adds layers to what could otherwise be a lazy bit. The question mark in delivery implies a kind of resigned openness. Gets a rewatch bonus for the callback at 09:00.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to yell. It's just... I feel like I'm a small nation that's been ignored by the Security Council, and everyone's passing resolutions about me without even letting me speak!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, that's... actually a pretty specific metaphor.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I've been preparing for Model U.N. since I was seven!

jokes.text: Jeff claims he was called 'model U.N. guy' in college, then immediately: 'Well, that's not-- don't research that.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to establish his model U.N. credentials to Professor Cligoris
jokes.punchline: 'Don't research that' — immediately walking back the claim, implying either it's false or the truth is embarrassing
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware Jeff joke. The quick retraction 'don't research that' is a funny indicator that the whole story was fabricated or more embarrassing than stated. It's character-specific: Jeff constantly performs a more impressive version of himself.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is... I Zambia'd the whole thing?

jokes.text: Professor Cligoris mistakes Jeff's advocacy for Annie for a reference to Clark M. Eichelburger: 'Really? So you're Clark M. Eichelburger. So I've had your photo around my neck since I was in high school.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is advocating for Annie Edison's claim to the model U.N. idea
jokes.punchline: Professor Cligoris has a fanatical devotion to the model U.N.'s historical founders — specifically Clark M. Eichelburger — that completely derails the conversation; 'photo around my neck' implies a locket-level devotion
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist character detail. The professor's obsession with Clark M. Eichelburger is exactly the kind of Greendale-specific eccentricity that makes the show feel lived-in. 'Photo around my neck since high school' is a funny specific — the level of devotion to a UN bureaucrat is perfectly Greendale.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I use condescension as a defense mechanism. It's easier to talk down to Annie than to actually acknowledge that I'm attracted to her.

jokes.text: Professor Cligoris: 'Is he your father or your lover?' — about Jeff's relationship with Annie
jokes.setup: Jeff has been speaking for Annie in a strangely invested way
jokes.punchline: The professor names the two most obvious interpretations of their dynamic — father or lover — which is both an accurate observation and a deeply uncomfortable one
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. It's an outside observer naming the Jeff/Annie dynamic with uncomfortable precision, landing on the 'father or lover' binary that the show has always danced around. The line is thematically resonant (the whole episode is about this dynamic) and funny because it cuts through all of Jeff's posturing. Gets a rewatch bonus because it directly seeds the later Jeff/Annie conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to stop calling you 'kiddo.' We're going to be... closer.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah. From now on, I'm calling you... Annie.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's my name.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This isn't working.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Nope.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Kiddo?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Much better.

jokes.text: Jeff and Annie's uncomfortable response to 'father or lover': 'We're friends. / Yeah. / Good friends. / Grown-up friends. / Yeah. / So. [long pause] We're friendly.'
jokes.setup: Professor Cligoris has just asked if Jeff is Annie's father or lover
jokes.punchline: Their increasingly desperate attempts to characterize their relationship ('Good friends. Grown-up friends. So. [pause] We're friendly.') each sound worse than the last — 'grown-up friends' is especially loaded given the context
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy. The rhythm of the exchange is perfect — each beat trying to establish normalcy and each one inadvertently making things more uncomfortable. 'Grown-up friends' is the best specific because it implies the opposite of what they mean. The pause before 'We're friendly' is the final deflation. Thematically central to the episode and very well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It was me. I did it. I'm sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No, it was me.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'm Spartacus!

jokes.text: Jeff's talking head strategy: 'So, the key to winning this thing is when in doubt, agree with Annie.' Shirley: 'That's sweet, Jeff.' Jeff: 'But everyone should just have fun.' Shirley: 'Then again, what's more fun than winning?'
jokes.setup: The group prepares strategy for the model U.N. competition
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a would-be inspirational speech; Shirley out-competes him in both the sweetness reading and the competitive drive in a single line
jokes.explanation: Good reversal. Jeff performs magnanimity ('agree with Annie,' 'just have fun') and Shirley calmly dismantles it with 'what's more fun than winning?' — revealing she's as competitive as anyone. Nice character moment for Shirley.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I am Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I am Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I am Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I am Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I am Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I am Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I am Spartacus!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, I actually did it. I really farted.

jokes.text: Pierce's Somalia research: 'Somalia has 1,900 miles of coastline, a government that knows its place, and all the guns and wives you can afford to buy. Why have I never heard of this paradise before?'
jokes.setup: The group is briefed on their assigned countries for the model U.N.
jokes.punchline: Pierce has approached Somalia not as a humanitarian context but as a consumer paradise — his genuine enthusiasm for a failed state's 'features' (buying guns and wives) is both horrifying and totally in character
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce joke. The structure — presenting Somalia as a Zagat review — is both inventive and character-perfect. 'A government that knows its place' is the funniest specific, implying Pierce's libertarian fantasy of minimal governance. 'Why have I never heard of this paradise before?' lands as a perfect kicker. This is Pierce at his most Pierce: oblivious, offensive, and completely earnest.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So I'll just stand here and mumble my whole plan, and then later they'll show a flashback of me explaining it clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not how real life works.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No. We're not on a TV show.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Then how do you explain the camera?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What camera?

jokes.text: Troy as Georgia (the country): 'That's right. Capital city Tbilisi, former member of the Soviet Union. And we kindly request y'all mind your Ps and Qs.'
jokes.setup: Troy has been assigned Georgia — the country, not the state — and is performing a character
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'Georgian' accent is indistinguishable from his regular Southern affect — 'y'all mind your Ps and Qs' as a diplomatic statement from the former Soviet republic
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific absurdism. Troy's representation of Georgia (the country) through the lens of Georgia (the state) is a consistent and funny bit. 'Y'all mind your Ps and Qs' as Soviet-bloc diplomatic language is a perfect fusion of the two Georgias.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What if we propose a joint Earth II initiative? We establish dual planetary governance systems, each country maintains sovereignty while sharing technological advancement protocols.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: That's... actually brilliant. The judges are eating it up.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Furthermore, we create a secondary Earth II as a backup, with a third Earth II as insurance for the backup, and a fourth Earth II exclusively for storing backups of the other Earth IIs.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, now you're just saying Earth II.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. I've solved world peace through recursive planetary duplication. It's foolproof.

jokes.text: Abed asks: 'Does two U.N.s mean there are two earths?' Professor: 'Uh, yeah. Sure, two earths.' Abed: 'Parallel earths in different galaxies or identical earths in parallel dimensions?' Professor: 'The latter one.'
jokes.setup: The model U.N. competition begins; the premise is two simultaneous UN bodies
jokes.punchline: Abed takes the logical implication of two U.N.s to its science-fiction conclusion — two Earths — and the professor, rather than correcting the premise, engages with it completely
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a perfect Community construction. Abed's literal, sci-fi-logic interpretation of the competition setup is in perfect character, but the genius is the professor's response: rather than explaining that it's a metaphor, he just says 'sure' and when pressed on specifics picks 'the latter one' with complete authority. The professor's capitulation to the insane premise is funnier than any correction could be. The joke also seeds the Earth II subplot. Rewatch bonus because Earth II pays off elaborately.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Cligoris
dialogue.line: Symbolic gestures are what the U.N. is actually about.

jokes.text: Professor Cligoris: 'Ready, set, peace.'
jokes.setup: The model U.N. competition is about to begin
jokes.punchline: Instead of 'ready, set, go' — 'ready, set, peace' — an earnest, slightly absurd invocation appropriate to the event
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Three words that capture Professor Cligoris's earnest idealism and the fundamental comedy of competitive world peace. The wordplay is simple but executed with ideal timing.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What are you doing to me? This feels like Operation!

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: It is Operation.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, why didn't you say so? I'm great at that game!

jokes.text: Pierce as Somalia offers Ethiopian refugees 'safe lodging and cool ocean breezes on its sand-swept beaches'
jokes.setup: Crisis: civil war in Ethiopia creating refugees; the U.N. asks who can take them
jokes.punchline: Pierce describes Somalia — a country with one of the world's worst humanitarian crises — as a resort destination for refugees, in Somali Chamber of Commerce language
jokes.explanation: Good extension of Pierce's Somalia bit. He's playing Somalia as a tourist-board representative for a failed state, and 'sand-swept beaches' and 'cool ocean breezes' are exactly the right absurd specifics. Works as a callback to his earlier Somalia enthusiasm.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: They took out my spare ribs!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your spare ribs?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Yeah, apparently I have more ribs than a normal person. The doctor said I'm like a side of beef.

jokes.text: Abed as Switzerland: 'And maybe at the peace summit we can discuss the possibility of opening a portal to Earth II.'
jokes.setup: The U.N. is working on the Ethiopia crisis; Switzerland proposes a peace summit
jokes.punchline: Abed uses the peace summit proposal as a Trojan horse to advance his Earth II agenda — staying completely in character as Switzerland but with an utterly Abed goal
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed move. He's identified a sci-fi premise within the game's logic and is now pursuing it with diplomatic precision. 'Can we put a pin in that, Switzerland?' from Annie is also funny — she's in character but also managing Abed. The Earth II running gag is building well.

jokes.text: Annie Edison: 'Can we put a pin in that, Switzerland? Earth II is out there, can't ignore it forever.'
jokes.setup: Abed has raised Earth II; Annie is trying to maintain order
jokes.punchline: Annie's first line ('can we put a pin in that') is her trying to shut it down; her second line ('Earth II is out there, can't ignore it forever') shows she's already half-bought into the premise
jokes.explanation: Nice beat in the Earth II running gag. Annie's capitulation — she says 'put a pin in that' but then validates the premise — is good character writing: she can't resist being organized even about sci-fi nonsense.

jokes.text: 'Ooh, China has money. Does anybody want some?' — Shirley as China
jokes.setup: The model U.N. is trying to solve the Ethiopia crisis
jokes.punchline: Shirley reduces China's global economic role to a cheerful offer to share money — like a potluck rather than international finance
jokes.explanation: Shirley's warmth and hospitality mapped onto China's financial leverage is a funny character-to-role incongruity. The simplicity of 'Does anybody want some?' applied to geopolitical economic power is good.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Oh! Damn, Pierce.' 'Ooh, that wasn't me.' 'I don't smell anything-- whup, I just got it.' 'Oh, it's in my mouth.'
jokes.setup: The model U.N. is going well; Pierce farts at a critical moment
jokes.punchline: The fart itself, then the extended group reaction — 'it's almost a solid,' 'it's in my mouth' — escalating descriptions that become increasingly revolting
jokes.explanation: Fart jokes are inherently low on the craft scale but this one earns partial credit for the escalating specificity ('almost a solid,' 'in my mouth') and for the structural purpose it serves — derailing the group at a critical moment, mirroring the real U.N.'s tendency to collapse on petty issues. Still, it's a fart joke. The craft scores reflect its reliance on cheap gross-out humor.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Get through it? It's almost a solid.'
jokes.setup: Jeff tells the group to 'get through' the fart smell and focus
jokes.punchline: Annie's specific descriptor — 'almost a solid' — which is disgusting but also shows Annie applying her characteristic precision to the most inappropriate subject
jokes.explanation: Fart joke elevated by character specificity. The fact that it's Annie who assesses it as 'almost a solid' — with her characteristic precise, earnest delivery — is funnier than if anyone else said it. The character integration saves this from being pure gross-out.

jokes.text: 'He's pulling my cage. I'm being pulled in my cage for no reason! Is anybody seeing this? Is the world seeing this? Are we facebooking this?'
jokes.setup: Troy has apparently arrested Britta (or put her in some kind of containment) for her Lionel Richie protest
jokes.punchline: Britta's immediate pivot to 'are we Facebooking this?' — turning her arrest into social media content — again skewers performative activism. Her outrage is real but its purpose is documentation.
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback to Britta's earlier Facebook distraction. Her arrested state becoming an opportunity for social media content is a precise satirical point about activist culture. 'Are we Facebooking this?' is the peak.

jokes.text: The chaos montage: rapid-fire 'Crisis alert' announcements overwhelm both U.N.s simultaneously — tuberculosis, famine, loose nukes, sinkholes, North Korea, coups — answered with simultaneous 'Resolved'/'Uruguay agrees'/'China will pay'
jokes.setup: Both model U.N.s are trying to solve the world's problems in competition
jokes.punchline: The problems come faster than any realistic response can handle, creating absurdist bureaucratic comedy — 'loose nukes — sinkhole — North Korea' — while the teams robotically keep resolving
jokes.explanation: The acceleration of global crises into a single breathless montage is excellent escalation comedy. It satirizes the actual UN's relationship with global catastrophe (everything becomes 'resolved' on paper) while providing kinetic comedic energy.

jokes.text: Security Chief tells Chang about a '1980s protestor' who gave him trouble — 'she incited a riot at the W.T.O. Got choked until she passed out. By some real cop with a real billyclub. Sometimes I wonder, you know?' — implying he's describing Britta's future
jokes.setup: Chang is confronted with Britta's protest and the Chief tells a cautionary tale
jokes.punchline: The Chief's 'Sometimes I wonder' at the end — wistful, implying he misses the days of real police brutality — is delivered as nostalgia for a more violent era of protest suppression
jokes.explanation: Dark joke about police brutality delivered with the Chief's characteristic deadpan. 'Sometimes I wonder, you know?' as a wistful kicker to a story about choking a protestor is an excellent dark beat. The Chief's character is defined by this — he's not villainous, just nostalgic for more violent times, which is funnier.

jokes.text: 'Uruguay sounds like "you're a gay."' / 'Uruguay kindly requests that Somalia stop pronouncing it "you're a gay."'
jokes.setup: Troy (Georgia) and Pierce (Somalia) are participating in the rapid-fire UN crisis resolution
jokes.punchline: Pierce's Uruguay pronunciation gag — with Troy formally requesting Pierce stop — adds a juvenile running gag to the chaos montage
jokes.explanation: The formal diplomatic language wrapping a juvenile pronunciation joke saves it from being completely cheap. 'Somalia kindly requests' as the framing for a 'you're a gay' joke is a mild upgrade on the base material. Still fairly low-effort wordplay.

jokes.text: 'Backyard barbecue!'
jokes.setup: In the rapid-fire chaos of global crises, Pierce (as Somalia) makes random proclamations
jokes.punchline: In the middle of solving North Korea and military coups, Pierce shouts 'Backyard barbecue!' — a completely non-diplomatic non-sequitur that suggests he's lost the thread entirely
jokes.explanation: Two words in the middle of diplomatic chaos. The randomness is precisely calibrated — Pierce would think 'barbecue' is a constructive diplomatic suggestion. Perfect non-sequitur economy.

jokes.text: Security Chief: 'Well, what are you waiting for? Go show that hippie how the world really works.' [pause] 'Aren't you forgetting something?' — implying Chang needs his trash can assignment
jokes.setup: The chief has motivated Chang to confront Britta; Chang is about to leave heroically
jokes.punchline: The implied pause: Chang has forgotten something. The 'something' is presumably his post at the trash can — his entire heroic moment undercut by his mundane garbage-can jurisdiction
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure. Chang's heroic moment is immediately undercut. The implication — that he's forgotten his trash can — doesn't need to be stated; the audience fills it in. Good economy in what's left unsaid.

jokes.text: Chang arrests Britta for spilling paint on a globe. Dean Pelton: 'Young lady, you spilled paint on a globe. You're as much a criminal as this idiot is a cop. None whatsoever.'
jokes.setup: Chang has brought Britta in as a criminal; they appear before the Dean
jokes.punchline: The Dean's parallel construction — Britta's crime = zero criminality; Chang's cop status = zero legitimacy — is both an insult and a logical observation
jokes.explanation: Efficient joke that serves multiple purposes — characterizes the Dean as sharp in a low-key way, undermines Chang's authority again, and deflates Britta's protest simultaneously. The parallel construction is clean.

jokes.text: Britta is asked if she intends to break any laws — she freezes, stumbles: 'I-I- Oh, my God. No, it's not that simple. I have a life now. I have a major and— Get out please. I have highlighters. Get out!'
jokes.setup: Britta is confronted with her activist identity vs. her new life at Greendale
jokes.punchline: She can't answer a simple yes-or-no question about breaking laws; her defense of her new life — 'I have highlighters' — is the perfect anti-climactic symbol of her capitulation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. 'I have highlighters' is a perfect callback to the opening scene where Britta's highlight/highlighter confusion established her new academic ambitions. Here, the highlighter represents her total surrender to conformity — it's the saddest possible defense of one's identity. The cringe of watching Britta unable to commit to either path is well-earned. High marks for character integration and structure.

jokes.text: Chang struggles to describe a parking gate arm to Jeff: 'Somebody broke that thing that comes down from the parking booth... It's like a gate, but it's just a stick. Comes down, from a hinge. Keeps the cars out. Goes up and down 90 degrees.'
jokes.setup: Chang approaches Jeff to report a problem
jokes.punchline: Chang cannot remember the word 'arm' — the extended circumlocution through 'thing,' 'gate,' 'stick,' '90 degrees' is both funny in itself and reveals Chang's limitations as a security professional
jokes.explanation: Good slow-burn joke. Chang's inability to say 'arm' grows funnier as it extends. The specificity of '90 degrees' as the angle of the gate arm is a funny detail — a precise measurement embedded in otherwise vague description. Gets slightly dragged down by its length.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'The arm?' [Cut to:] 'Ooh, point goes to red team.'
jokes.setup: Chang has been circumlocuting about the parking gate arm for over twenty seconds
jokes.punchline: Jeff's guess ('The arm?') cuts to the model U.N., where it's been counted as a contribution — the word 'arm' has resolved both conversations simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best comedic construction. Two completely separate storylines are resolved by the same word — 'The arm?' — through a cut that makes the connection. Jeff's confused answer to Chang accidentally scores a point in the model U.N. The structure is architecturally elegant: the extended Chang setup (which seemed like padding) was necessary to build the tension that makes the crosscut pay off. This is craft-forward sitcom writing at its best. The economy is extraordinary — the entire joke lands on two words and a cut.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'So whoever actually died a few months ago, 'fess up so we can put a stake through your heart.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has farted again; the group is suffering
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response to the fart situation frames it as a supernatural death-smell situation — 'whoever actually died' implies the smell is a ghost fart from beyond the grave
jokes.explanation: Good Jeff line — the vampire metaphor applied to a fart is a funny escalation. Character-specific in that Jeff reaches for a deadpan literary register even when talking about flatulence.

jokes.text: 'How is this still happening? I can't remember what regular air smells like.'
jokes.setup: The fart situation is continuing; the group is trying to maintain focus
jokes.punchline: Jeff's existential complaint — 'can't remember what regular air smells like' — treats a temporary inconvenience with the gravity of long-term trauma
jokes.explanation: Saves the fart material somewhat — Jeff's disproportionate suffering is funnier than the fart itself. 'Can't remember what regular air smells like' applied to what is apparently a prolonged event is a good line.

jokes.text: Annie loses her composure completely: 'I want to win! And you! You suck! You're a stupid, ugly poopface! I'm better than you!'
jokes.setup: Annie has been maintaining a composed facade; the competition pressure and Jeff's attitude crack her
jokes.punchline: The devolution from coherent argument to 'stupid, ugly poopface' — the contrast between Annie's usual articulate intelligence and playground-grade insults is the joke
jokes.explanation: Annie's meltdown is a satisfying character moment. 'Stupid, ugly poopface' works because it's such a specific regression — not just childish but specifically kindergarten-level. The contrast with her usual vocabulary (she was giving Yalta analysis twenty minutes earlier) is the comedic engine. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Annie, stop. You're acting like a little schoolgirl and not in a hot way.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to calm Annie down from her outburst
jokes.punchline: He adds the qualifier 'not in a hot way' — which reveals his usual framework for thinking about Annie is 'hot schoolgirl,' making the correction worse than the original statement
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Jeff's self-correction ('not in a hot way') inadvertently exposes the creepiness he's trying to disavow — the 'hot way' exists as a category in his mind, which is exactly the problem the episode is interrogating. The structure is a classic 'the correction makes it worse' construction. High marks for character integration: this line could ONLY come from Jeff. Directly feeds the subsequent Jeff/Annie conversation.

jokes.text: 'Okay. Uh, that made me sound creepy. But--but here's the thing.' [extended awkward pause before Jeff and Annie walk off to talk privately]
jokes.setup: Jeff has just said 'not in a hot way' and the whole room has heard it
jokes.punchline: Jeff's acknowledgment that he 'sounds creepy' and his attempt to pivot is interrupted by an awkward pause — the pause itself is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good beat that extends the previous joke. Jeff's self-aware acknowledgment of the creepiness is both comedic and sets up the earnest conversation to follow. The 'But--but here's the thing' trailing off into silence is a funny specific.

jokes.text: Annie's talking head after the meltdown: 'Don't look at me. If embarrassment were bountiful zinc deposits, I'd be Zambia.'
jokes.setup: Annie has just had a complete public meltdown at the model U.N.
jokes.punchline: She expresses embarrassment through a geography/natural-resources metaphor that's entirely appropriate to the model U.N. context — 'Zambia' as the punchline is unexpected and specific
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke, by a significant margin. 'If embarrassment were bountiful zinc deposits, I'd be Zambia' is extraordinary on multiple levels: (1) It's character-specific in the extreme — Annie expresses shame through academic/geographical knowledge, maintaining her Annie-ness even in humiliation. (2) The metaphor construction is unusual and inventive — nobody has ever used 'zinc deposits' as a unit of embarrassment before. (3) 'Zambia' is the perfect specific — a real zinc-producing country, chosen for both accuracy and sonic comedy. (4) It's perfectly economical. (5) It's highly quotable and adaptable as a construction. This is a rare moment where the writing elevates a simple emotion (embarrassment) into something genuinely surprising. Comparable to the 9.5 anchor in terms of originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'There's nothing to be Zambia about, Annie.'
jokes.setup: Annie has just said 'I'd be Zambia'
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately uses 'Zambia' as a verb/adjective in place of 'embarrassed' — riffing on her metaphor
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. Jeff adopts Annie's metaphor and extends it, turning 'Zambia' into a verb ('nothing to be Zambia about'). It's a sweet character moment — Jeff engaging with Annie's language — and very funny because the construction is grammatically absurd but completely comprehensible. Gets rewatch bonus because the callback rewards attentive viewing.

jokes.text: '- Nope. I can't, no. - Nope, that's gross. That feels gross.'
jokes.setup: Annie has asked 'Can't we?' (keep the paternalistic close dynamic) after Jeff's speech about needing to grow up
jokes.punchline: Both simultaneously and emphatically saying 'Nope' — a shared recognition that actually continuing the 'kiddo' dynamic feels wrong now that they've named it
jokes.explanation: The mutual 'Nope' and 'that feels gross' is a perfect button on the scene. Having named the dynamic, neither can unsee it. The simultaneous agreement is funny because they're both equally uncomfortable — suggesting the speech did exactly what Jeff intended: made the relationship too conscious to maintain.

jokes.text: Annie apologizes to the group for putting them through the competition, then asks: 'Would it help if I said [pause] I farted?'
jokes.setup: Annie is making a sincere apology to the group for the competition drama
jokes.punchline: She offers a Spartacus-style self-sacrifice — claiming responsibility for the fart that disrupted their competition — as an act of group bonding
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke. The setup is a sincere emotional apology, making the pivot to 'I farted' completely unexpected. The logic — that claiming the fart is an act of self-sacrifice for group unity — is both absurd and weirdly touching. It also sets up the Spartacus scene.

jokes.text: The group's Spartacus moment: each member claims 'I farted' one by one, with Troy claiming it twice and Abed declaring 'I'm farting now'
jokes.setup: Annie claimed responsibility for the fart; Jeff says 'Annie, no. I can't let you fall on that sword because... I farted.'
jokes.punchline: The Spartacus structure — everyone claiming the fart — builds absurdly, culminating in Abed's 'I'm farting now' (present tense, implying active participation) and Troy claiming it twice
jokes.explanation: Very well-executed parody of the Spartacus 'I am Spartacus' scene, applied to fart ownership. The structure works because (a) it's a recognizable cinematic callback, (b) each individual claim lands as a small beat, and (c) Abed's 'I'm farting now' is the perfect escalation — he's not just claiming past responsibility but actively joining in. 'Wait, why are you still here?' as a coda implies the actual farter (Pierce) has stayed to watch.

jokes.text: 'Annie, no.' / 'I can't let you fall on that sword because...' / [each person claims responsibility] '...I farted.' / 'No, I farted.' / 'I farted.' — The Spartacus sequence
jokes.setup: Annie has claimed she farted to take the blame; Jeff says she can't take the blame
jokes.punchline: Everyone begins claiming they farted in a parody of the Spartacus 'I am Spartacus' scene — which makes no logical sense (everyone claiming credit for the same fart) but is emotionally satisfying
jokes.explanation: A genuinely heartwarming and funny Spartacus parody — the absurdity of everyone claiming a fart as an act of group solidarity is exactly the kind of elevated-lowbrow comedy Community excels at. The structure is perfect: the more people claim it, the funnier and more touching it becomes simultaneously. 'Guys, I wasn't doing the Spartacus thing. I farted.' from one character (Pierce, presumably) is the kicker that completes the joke.

jokes.text: Abed's plan: 'It's simple, really. First we...' [mumbles inaudibly] Jeff: 'Abed, what did I tell you? You can't just mumble nonsense. No one's cutting away. Okay, fine, here's my actual plan.'
jokes.setup: Abed proposes a plan to win the competition
jokes.punchline: Abed mumbles because he expects the show to cut away (a TV convention where characters whisper plans and the camera cuts to the execution); Jeff breaks the fourth wall to inform him 'no one's cutting away' — forcing Abed to actually explain the plan
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta joke, one of the episode's best. Abed's behavior is entirely consistent with his character — he lives inside TV logic and expects the show to follow TV conventions. Jeff's 'no one's cutting away' is both a character moment (Jeff's pragmatism) and a meta-textual joke about how TV plans work. The joke is inventive because it names a specific TV grammar convention (the whispered-plan cutaway) and then refuses to honor it. High originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Britta's note promising disruption of the model U.N. — 'She's promising to disrupt the model...U.N.' / pause reading / 'Security!'
jokes.setup: Britta has sent a note to Annie promising to cause a disruption
jokes.punchline: The note says she'll disrupt 'campus Security' — Britta's promised act of rebellion is to mess with Troy's garbage can duties, not the actual event
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — the pause on 'model...U.N.' lets the audience think she's disrupting the competition, then 'Security!' reveals she's disrupting Troy. Britta's radicalism targeting the most minor possible 'institution' (Greendale's one-man security operation) is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Annie Kim calls the Earth II gambit 'a technical act of aggression' and refuses to recognize it — winning the literal competition while losing the symbolic one
jokes.setup: Annie Edison/Abed offer a symbolic peace deal via Earth II; Annie Kim recognizes it's a trick
jokes.punchline: Annie Kim is correct and logical — refusing to recognize the authority is the right move — but as Professor Cligoris notes, it means she's won the game and lost the spirit of the UN
jokes.explanation: Thematically elegant joke. Annie Kim's logical refusal is the right move tactically but Professor Cligoris's ruling — 'Blue U.N. wins' — rewards the symbolic gesture. The joke is that in model U.N. (as in real diplomacy), earnest useless idealism beats cold logic. It's also a satisfying character defeat for Annie Kim: she was too smart to lose correctly.

jokes.text: 'You're a fool. Your ultimatum is itself a technical act of aggression. If we simply refuse to recognize your authority, we still remain ahead and you lose.'
jokes.setup: Abed/Annie Edison's U.N. has proposed forming a 'United United Nations' and conceding the win to achieve a larger symbolic victory
jokes.punchline: Annie Kim correctly identifies this as a manipulation and chooses the technical win — a logically defensible decision that is also the least generous possible read of the situation
jokes.explanation: Annie Kim's logical ruthlessness is consistent with her character. The comedy is in her being completely right while also missing the point — she wins the game and loses the metaphor.

jokes.text: 'But you win a simple game. The larger symbolic victory will be ours.' / 'Oh la la.' / 'We refuse.' / 'I'll take the real victory.'
jokes.setup: Annie Edison claims the 'symbolic victory' even as Annie Kim takes the actual win
jokes.punchline: Professor Cligoris's 'Oh la la' is a perfect deadpan reaction to two teenagers arguing about symbolic versus real victories in a school competition. 'I'll take the real victory' as Annie Kim's flat final word is impeccably cold.
jokes.explanation: The 'Oh la la' from the professor is excellent — his bemusement at the intensity of a school exercise. 'I'll take the real victory' as Annie Kim's exit line is satisfying character work.

jokes.text: Professor Cligoris's ruling speech: 'A logical, effective, common sense move, Annie Kim. One which flies in the very face of the United Nations itself, a fundamentally symbolic organization founded on the principles of high-minded rhetoric and empty gestures. Blue U.N. wins.'
jokes.setup: Annie Kim has made the strategically correct move of refusing the Earth II offer
jokes.punchline: Professor Cligoris rules against her because pragmatic realism is antithetical to the UN's actual purpose — 'high-minded rhetoric and empty gestures' as the founding principles
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most Community-esque jokes. The ruling is both a satisfying episode resolution and a genuinely sharp satirical observation about the UN. 'Founded on the principles of high-minded rhetoric and empty gestures' is excellent writing — it's simultaneously the UN's mission statement and an indictment of it. High quotability; the line works as a standalone observation outside the show.

jokes.text: Britta's second Lionel Richie 'Hello' protest — this time outside the model U.N., Chang pursues her across campus in a golf cart while she sings
jokes.setup: Britta has promised to disrupt the model U.N.; Chang has been sent to stop her
jokes.punchline: The disruption is Lionel Richie again — she hasn't upgraded her protest tactics; the chase/arrest becomes a full physical comedy sequence set to 'Hello'
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the Lionel Richie running gag. The escalation — now there's a golf cart chase — maintains the absurdism while adding visual comedy. The choice to repeat the same song rather than escalate to something edgier is true to Britta's character and funny.

jokes.text: Chang arrests Britta. Britta: 'I knew you'd come.' Chang: 'You're so busted.'
jokes.setup: Chang has chased Britta down during her protest
jokes.punchline: Britta greets her arrest as a heroic moment ('I knew you'd come') — she's finally gotten her protest arrest. Chang's 'You're so busted' deflates it completely
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. Britta has finally achieved her protest credential (arrest by campus security while singing Lionel Richie) and treats it as vindication. The gap between her romanticized vision of activism and the mundane reality is the persistent engine of the B-plot.

jokes.text: Tag scene: Chang is in what appears to be a medical context. 'I told you to stop playing Operation on me! I'm not your damn board game! At least you didn't get my spare ribs.'
jokes.setup: Post-credits or tag scene; context implies someone has been using Chang as a human Operation board game
jokes.punchline: 'At least you didn't get my spare ribs' — using the actual Operation game piece names as anatomical references, implying he's genuinely been played on as a board game
jokes.explanation: Good tag scene. The 'spare ribs' Operation reference is funny because it bridges anatomical reality and the game piece name. The absurdism of someone actually playing Operation on Chang fits his character as someone who invites abuse. Good economy for a tag.

tmdb_overview: As Annie competes with an overachieving rival in a Model United Nations competition, Jeff wrestles with his feelings for his ambitious friend.
insight: Escalation-driven cringe comedy carries a mid-tier episode through 46 jokes in 46 minutes.
